hints: Look closely at the shapes in the diagram. Q is the thin thread winding around things, P is the cluster of round beads it winds around, and R is the single flat oval at the base.
Remember what a nucleosome is made of and what has to happen to all those beads on a string during prophase to make a thick, visible chromatid.
walkthrough:
**Identify P, Q and R from the diagram**

First, let's read the picture like a biologist. Q is the continuous double helix thread of DNA. P is the group of 8 round histone proteins that Q wraps around. R is the single linker histone (H1) that sits at the base and holds the DNA in place.

Together, P + Q + R = a nucleosome, the beads on a string unit.

**Recall what prophase must do**

In prophase of mitosis, the long thin chromatin must condense a huge amount. Those nucleosome strings do not stay loose. They coil, fold and supercoil again and again to pack tightly.

This higher level folding is what turns loose chromatin into a thick, short, visible chromatid.

**Pick the statement that describes this correctly**

Option D is the only one that gets all three labels right and describes the real prophase event. Linked nucleosomes (P and R with DNA Q) form strands that fold and twist together to build a chromatid. Lovely, that is exactly condensation.

options.A: Q is DNA, that part is right, but it wraps around P (the histone octamer), not around R. R is just the single linker histone.
options.B: P and Q do pack closer during condensation, but they do not condense around R. R is only a small linker protein, not the scaffold for the whole chromosome.
options.C: It is true histones are protein and help DNA fit in the nucleus, but R is not part of the wrapping core. DNA wraps around P, while R just seals the nucleosome.
options.D: Correct. P (core histones) plus R (linker histone) plus Q (DNA) make nucleosomes, and in prophase these strands fold, coil and supercoil to form a condensed chromatid.
